claims.text: Increasing Nickel content enhances the chemical stability of the FCC phase during thermal aging.
Enhanced FCC-phase stability delays the formation of brittle phases.
Delaying brittle-phase formation promotes sustained dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Sustained dislocation-mediated plasticity helps retain toughness.
The baseline high-entropy alloy has a mixed microstructure containing FCC and other phases and is vulnerable to phase transformation and toughness loss during thermal aging.
Enhanced FCC stability prevents or retards transformation to brittle phases.
Enhanced FCC stability maintains favorable phase-boundary characteristics.
Added Nickel acts as an FCC-phase stabilizer during thermal exposure.
Nickel addition reduces the kinetics of brittle-phase precipitation or transformation.
Stabilized FCC-containing microstructures help maintain dislocation mobility.
Maintaining dislocation mobility delays embrittlement and sustains high fracture toughness.
After thermal aging, the Nickel-enriched alloy will retain a higher fracture toughness, measured as KIC, than the lower-Nickel baseline.
After thermal aging, the Nickel-enriched alloy will retain a more stable FCC microstructure than the lower-Nickel baseline.
The lower-Nickel baseline undergoes microstructural instability and toughness degradation during thermal aging.
The proposed behavior is expected to apply primarily to high-entropy alloys in which FCC is the predominant phase under engineering-relevant thermal aging.
The proposed behavior may not transfer to ultra-high-temperature regimes or degradation modes other than thermal aging.
Grain growth and interactions with other alloying elements may modulate the Nickel-dependent toughness response.
